questions.question: Using a two-country example, distinguish absolute from comparative advantage and show why trade benefits both countries even when one is better at producing everything.
questions.expected_answer: Absolute advantage means producing a good with fewer resources — more output per worker. Comparative advantage means having the lowest opportunity cost — giving up least by producing that good rather than another — and it, not absolute advantage, determines the gains from trade. Example: with the same resources South Africa can produce 100 tons of maize or 50 of steel; Germany 120 of maize or 240 of steel. Germany is absolutely better at both. But a ton of steel costs South Africa two tons of maize while it costs Germany only half a ton; a ton of maize costs Germany two tons of steel but South Africa only half a ton of steel. Germany sacrifices least in steel, South Africa least in maize. If each specialises where its sacrifice is lowest and they trade at a rate between the two opportunity costs — say one for one — both countries consume beyond their own production possibilities. Trade needs only differences in relative costs, not superiority.

questions.question: Describe the accounts of the balance of payments, placing typical South African items, and explain how the rand's exchange rate is established on the foreign exchange market.
questions.expected_answer: The current account records present trade and income: merchandise exports (minerals, vehicles, fruit) and imports (oil, machinery, electronics) whose difference is the trade balance; services such as transport and tourism (a foreign tourist's spending here is a service export); income flows like dividends and interest; and current transfers. The small capital transfer account records items like debt forgiveness. The financial account shows how net imports are paid for: direct investment (a foreign firm building a factory), portfolio investment (foreign purchases of shares and bonds — hot money, easily reversed) and other investment (loans and deposits). The SARB's gold and foreign-exchange reserves absorb the remaining difference so the statement balances; a current-account deficit requires a financial-account surplus. The exchange rate is the rand price of foreign currency, set where the demand for dollars (importers, travellers, firms paying dividends or repaying dollar loans, residents investing abroad) meets the supply of dollars (export earnings, arriving tourists, foreign investment inflows). Demand shifting right — say a doubled oil price — raises the rand price of the dollar (depreciation); supply shifting right — a commodity boom or investment inflow — lowers it (appreciation). Devaluation and revaluation refer only to deliberate changes under a fixed-rate system; South Africa's rand floats freely.

questions.question: Explain what a balance-of-payments disequilibrium is and evaluate the four channels through which a persistent deficit can be corrected.
questions.expected_answer: A disequilibrium exists when deficits or surpluses persist beyond what normal financing can carry; persistent deficits drain reserves and accumulate foreign debt, while persistent surpluses mean consuming less than the country earns. Four correction channels: (1) exchange-rate adjustment — under floating, excess demand for foreign currency depreciates the rand, making exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home so the gap narrows; cost: imported inflation, and volumes respond only with a lag. (2) Demand management — contractionary monetary and fiscal policy cools spending and thus imports, and higher rates attract financing inflows; cost: slower growth and higher unemployment. (3) Direct controls — tariffs, quotas and exchange control ration imports and foreign currency; cost: retaliation, evasion, inefficiency, and WTO constraints. (4) Borrowing and reserves — drawing down reserves or IMF loans buys time; cost: conditionality and debt. A surplus is corrected in reverse: allow appreciation, expand domestic demand, liberalise imports. The best answers match the tool to the cause: an overvalued currency calls for channel one, an overheated economy for channel two.
